rules.title: Prohibition on Common Pricing Algorithms in Restraint of Trade
rules.effectiveDateQuote: Approved by Governor October 06, 2025. Filed with Secretary of State October 06, 2025.
rules.requirement: It is unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination, trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce. It is also unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm if they coerce another person to set or adopt a recommended price or commercial term recommended by that algorithm for the same or similar products or services in California.
rules.quotedSpan: It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter. (b) It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm if the person coerces another person to set or adopt a recommended price or commercial term recommended by the common pricing algorithm for the same or similar products or services in the jurisdiction of this state.
rules.coverageDescription: Applies to all persons and entities in California that use or distribute common pricing algorithms affecting rental housing prices or commercial terms.
exemptions: End consumers of products or services are excluded from the definition of "person" under the statute
warnings: The statute defines 'common pricing algorithm' broadly to include any methodology using competitor data to recommend, align, stabilize, set, or otherwise influence a price or commercial term; application to rental housing algorithms depends on whether they use competitor rental data and whether they are used as part of a restraint of trade or conspiracy
The term 'coerces' is not defined in the statute and may require judicial interpretation to determine what conduct constitutes unlawful coercion

Statute applies to 'persons' which includes natural persons, partnerships, corporations, and other business entities, but excludes end consumers; it is unclear whether individual landlords or property managers using algorithms would be subject
The statute is part of antitrust law (Cartwright Act) and violations may be pursued as crimes; civil applicability to landlord-tenant disputes is not explicitly addressed
Effective date is the Governor's signature date; no delayed implementation period specified

AB 325 is a broad antitrust law directed at pricing algorithms generally, not specifically at rental housing; its application to rent-setting algorithms and landlord coordination on rental prices depends on fact-specific analysis of whether a particular algorithm or practice violates the statutory prohibitions
The statute uses terms like 'coerce,' 'recommend,' 'align,' and 'stabilize' that may require judicial interpretation in the rental housing context

No specific exemptions for landlords, property managers, or rental housing providers are stated in the statute; uncertainty exists about whether routine use of neutral rent-setting tools or market-rate analyses would trigger liability
